questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which technique is most suitable for separating a mixture of common salt and water?
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves in water, so filtration cannot separate them; distillation evaporates the water and condenses it, leaving the salt behind.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the best criterion for testing the purity of a crystalline solid?
questions.explanation: Pure crystalline substances melt sharply at a fixed temperature; impurities lower and broaden the melting point range.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Chromatography is most useful for separating
options: components of a mixture of dyes with different solubilities
a solid from a liquid by size
a salt from its solution by evaporation
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates substances based on differing rates of movement (solubility/adsorption) through a stationary medium, ideal for dyes and pigments.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Sublimation is used to separate a mixture of iodine and sand because
options: iodine changes directly from solid to vapour on heating while sand does not
sand dissolves in water but iodine does not
questions.explanation: Iodine sublimes (solid to gas without melting) on gentle heating, leaving the non-volatile sand behind; the vapour is then cooled to recover solid iodine.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which method separates two miscible liquids with different boiling points?
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to separate liquids of close but different boiling points by repeated vaporisation-condensation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A mixture of iron filings and sulphur powder is best separated by
options: using a magnet to attract the iron filings
questions.explanation: Iron is ferromagnetic while sulphur is not, so a magnet physically separates them without any chemical change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which separation technique relies on differences in density between two immiscible liquids?
questions.explanation: A separating funnel allows the denser liquid to be run off from the bottom while the less dense liquid remains on top.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Water obtained by fractional distillation of a salt solution is described as
options: distilled water, free of dissolved salts
questions.explanation: Distillation vaporises only the water, leaving the non-volatile salt behind, so the condensed liquid is pure (distilled) water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The Law of Definite Proportions states that
options: a pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed mass ratio
the mass of reactants equals the mass of products
gases combine in simple whole-number volume ratios
equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules
questions.explanation: This law (Proust's Law) states that a given chemical compound always contains its constituent elements in fixed proportion by mass, regardless of source.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which law is illustrated by carbon forming both CO and CO2, where the masses of oxygen combining with a fixed mass of carbon are in a simple ratio of 1:2?
questions.explanation: The Law of Multiple Proportions applies when one element forms more than one compound with another, and the masses of the second element combining with a fixed mass of the first are in a ratio of small whole numbers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Avogadro's Law states that
options: gases expand by 1/273 of their volume for every degree rise in temperature
the volume of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure
mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules
questions.explanation: Avogadro's Law links gas volume directly to the number of moles (particles) present, independent of the gas's identity, at fixed temperature and pressure.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: How many moles of oxygen atoms are present in 0.5 mole of CO2?
questions.explanation: Each CO2 molecule contains 2 oxygen atoms, so 0.5 mole of CO2 contains 0.5 x 2 = 1.0 mole of oxygen atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the relative molecular mass of Na2CO3? (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What mass of calcium (Ca = 40) contains the same number of atoms as 8 g of oxygen (O = 16)?
questions.explanation: 8 g of oxygen = 8/16 = 0.5 mole of atoms. 0.5 mole of Ca = 0.5 x 40 = 20 g, since equal moles contain equal numbers of atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Calculate the number of moles in 11 g of CO2. (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CO2 = 44 g/mol. Moles = mass/molar mass = 11/44 = 0.25 mole.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What volume of oxygen (at s.t.p.) is required to completely burn 2 moles of carbon to form CO2? (Molar volume = 22.4 dm3 at s.t.p.)
questions.explanation: C + O2 -> CO2, so 2 moles of carbon require 2 moles of O2. Volume = 2 x 22.4 = 44.8 dm3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An oxide of a metal M has the formula M2O3 and a relative molecular mass of 102. What is the relative atomic mass of M? (O = 16)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The empirical formula of a compound containing 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen, and 53.3% oxygen by mass is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Moles: C = 40/12 = 3.33, H = 6.7/1 = 6.7, O = 53.3/16 = 3.33. Dividing by the smallest (3.33) gives C:H:O = 1:2:1, so the empirical formula is CH2O.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: According to the kinetic theory of matter, particles in a gas
options: are arranged in a regular, orderly lattice
are tightly packed and vibrate about fixed positions
move randomly at high speed with negligible forces of attraction between them
questions.explanation: Gas particles are far apart, move rapidly and randomly in all directions, and experience very weak intermolecular forces compared to solids and liquids.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Boyle's Law states that at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is
options: directly proportional to its absolute temperature
questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: PV = constant at constant temperature, so as pressure increases, volume decreases proportionally.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A gas occupies 400 cm3 at a pressure of 760 mmHg. What volume will it occupy at 950 mmHg, assuming constant temperature?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Charles's Law relates the volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure to its
questions.explanation: Charles's Law: V/T = constant at constant pressure, meaning volume increases directly with absolute temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A sample of gas has a volume of 200 cm3 at 27 degC. What volume will it occupy at 127 degC, at constant pressure?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Graham's Law of diffusion states that the rate of diffusion of a gas is
options: directly proportional to its pressure only
inversely proportional to the square root of its density
questions.explanation: Graham's Law: lighter (less dense) gases diffuse faster, with rate inversely proportional to the square root of density (or molar mass).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which gas diffuses faster, hydrogen (M = 2) or oxygen (M = 32), and by what approximate factor?
options: They diffuse at the same rate
questions.explanation: Rate ratio = sqrt(M_oxygen/M_hydrogen) = sqrt(32/2) = sqrt(16) = 4, so hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster than oxygen.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures states that the total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals
options: the average of the partial pressures
the partial pressure of the heaviest gas only
the sum of the partial pressures each gas would exert alone
the product of the partial pressures
questions.explanation: Dalton's Law: total pressure = sum of individual partial pressures of each gas in the mixture, assuming no chemical reaction occurs between them.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In the ideal gas equation PV = nRT, what does 'n' represent?
questions.explanation: In PV = nRT, n is the number of moles, P is pressure, V is volume, R is the universal gas constant, and T is absolute temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which condition is defined as standard temperature and pressure (s.t.p.) in gas law calculations?
questions.explanation: Standard temperature and pressure is conventionally defined as 273 K (0 degC) and 760 mmHg (1 atmosphere), at which 1 mole of gas occupies 22.4 dm3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which subatomic particle has a negligible mass and carries a negative charge?
questions.explanation: The electron has a charge of -1 and a mass about 1/1836 that of a proton, making its mass essentially negligible in atomic mass calculations.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of
questions.explanation: Isotopes share the same atomic number (protons) but differ in mass number due to differing numbers of neutrons in the nucleus.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An atom of an element has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. What is its mass number?
questions.explanation: Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the electronic configuration of an element with atomic number 12?
questions.explanation: Electrons fill shells in order (2, 8, 8, ...); for 12 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, and the remaining 2 in the third shell, giving 2,8,2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties because they have the same
options: number of electrons in their outermost shell
questions.explanation: Chemical behaviour is largely determined by valence (outermost shell) electrons, and elements in the same group share the same number of these.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally
options: increases due to more electron shells
decreases due to increasing nuclear charge pulling electrons closer
increases due to decreasing nuclear charge
questions.explanation: Across a period, protons increase while electrons are added to the same shell, so the stronger nuclear pull draws the electron cloud inward, shrinking atomic radius.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An electrovalent (ionic) bond is formed by
options: sharing of a pair of electrons donated by only one atom
complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another
overlap of metal ion cores in a sea of electrons
sharing of a pair of electrons between two atoms
questions.explanation: In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred completely, typically from a metal to a non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A coordinate (dative covalent) bond differs from an ordinary covalent bond in that
options: it only occurs between two identical atoms
electrons are transferred rather than shared
both shared electrons come from only one of the bonding atoms
no electrons are shared at all
questions.explanation: In a coordinate bond, one atom (the donor) supplies both electrons of the shared pair, as seen in the formation of the ammonium ion, NH4+.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Metallic bonding is best described as
options: a lattice of positive metal ions held together by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons
electron transfer between two metal atoms
a shared pair of electrons between two metal atoms
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding involves positive ion cores fixed in a lattice, surrounded by mobile, delocalised valence electrons that conduct heat and electricity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Hydrogen bonding is best described as
options: a relatively strong intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom and a lone pair on another electronegative atom
an ionic bond involving a hydrogen ion
a covalent bond within a hydrogen molecule
a weak van der Waals force present in all molecules
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds form when hydrogen, covalently bonded to N, O, or F, is attracted to a lone pair on a nearby electronegative atom, explaining water's unusually high boiling point.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the approximate percentage by volume of nitrogen in the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and small amounts of carbon dioxide, argon, and other gases.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which gas is primarily responsible for the greenhouse effect and global warming when released in excess?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide traps outgoing infrared radiation in the atmosphere, and its build-up from fossil fuel combustion drives enhanced global warming.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Temporary hardness of water is caused mainly by dissolved
questions.explanation: Temporary hardness arises from calcium and magnesium hydrogen carbonates, which decompose on boiling to form insoluble carbonates, removing the hardness.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Permanent hardness of water, unlike temporary hardness, cannot be removed by
questions.explanation: Permanent hardness is caused by calcium and magnesium sulphates/chlorides, which do not decompose on boiling, unlike the bicarbonates causing temporary hardness.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which process is commonly used in large-scale municipal treatment to purify drinking water?
questions.explanation: Water treatment plants typically use sedimentation to settle suspended solids, filtration to remove finer particles, and chlorination to kill pathogens.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of these is a major atmospheric pollutant produced by burning fossil fuels containing sulphur impurities?
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide from burning sulphur-containing fuels dissolves in atmospheric moisture to form sulphurous and sulphuric acids, contributing to acid rain.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A saturated solution is one that
options: contains less solute than it can possibly dissolve
has no solute dissolved in it
contains more solute than a supersaturated solution at the same temperature
contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in the solvent at a given temperature
questions.explanation: In a saturated solution, undissolved solute exists in dynamic equilibrium with the dissolved solute, at the maximum concentration for that temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A supersaturated solution is best described as one that
options: contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution would normally hold at that temperature
cannot dissolve any more solute under any condition
questions.explanation: Supersaturated solutions are unstable and are usually prepared by cooling a hot saturated solution carefully so excess solute stays dissolved without crystallising.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: On a solubility curve, the solubility of most solid solutes in water generally
questions.explanation: For most ionic solids, solubility rises with temperature because increased thermal energy helps break the solute's lattice and disperse ions into solution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The solubility of a solute at a given temperature is typically expressed as
options: the melting point of the solute
the number of solvent molecules present
the total volume of the solution
the mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent to form a saturated solution
questions.explanation: Solubility is conventionally quoted as grams of solute per 100 g of solvent at a stated temperature, allowing direct comparison across substances.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: If 40 g of a salt dissolves in 100 g of water at 60 degC to form a saturated solution, and the solution is cooled to 20 degC where solubility is 25 g per 100 g of water, how much salt crystallises out?
questions.explanation: Excess salt that can no longer stay dissolved crystallises: 40 g - 25 g = 15 g of salt is deposited as the solution cools.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Gases generally become _____ soluble in water as temperature increases.
questions.explanation: Unlike most solids, gas solubility in liquids decreases with rising temperature, which is why warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An acid is best defined as a substance that
questions.explanation: By the Bronsted-Lowry definition, an acid is a proton (H+) donor, producing H3O+ ions when dissolved in water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A base that is soluble in water is specifically called
questions.explanation: All alkalis are bases, but only soluble bases (e.g., NaOH, KOH) are termed alkalis, since they release hydroxide ions into solution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14. A solution with pH 7 is considered
questions.explanation: pH 7 indicates equal concentrations of H+ and OH- ions, characteristic of pure water and neutral solutions; below 7 is acidic, above 7 is alkaline.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which indicator turns red in acidic solution and blue in alkaline solution?
questions.explanation: Litmus is a classic acid-base indicator: it turns red in acid and blue in alkali, making it a simple qualitative test.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Neutralization is the reaction between an acid and a base to produce
options: a salt and a gas only
questions.explanation: The general equation for neutralization is: acid + base -> salt + water, as in HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A salt formed by only partial replacement of the acidic hydrogen atoms of a dibasic acid is called
questions.explanation: An acid salt, e.g., NaHSO4, still contains a replaceable hydrogen atom because not all acidic hydrogens of the parent acid were neutralised.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a normal salt?
questions.explanation: A normal salt results from complete replacement of all replaceable hydrogen ions of an acid by a metal or ammonium ion, leaving no acidic hydrogen, as in NaCl.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In an acid-base titration, the point at which the acid exactly neutralises the base is called the
questions.explanation: The equivalence point (often signalled by an indicator colour change, the end point) is where moles of acid and base have reacted in exact stoichiometric proportion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: 25 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 HCl exactly neutralises 20 cm3 of NaOH solution. What is the concentration of the NaOH?
questions.explanation: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O (1:1 ratio). Moles HCl = 0.025 x 0.1 = 0.0025 mol = moles NaOH. Concentration NaOH = 0.0025/0.020 = 0.125 mol/dm3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which gas is evolved when a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid?
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acids to release carbon dioxide gas, which turns limewater milky, e.g., CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Oxidation is best defined in terms of electron transfer as
questions.explanation: By the electronic definition, oxidation is loss of electrons (OIL: Oxidation Is Loss), while reduction is gain of electrons (RIG).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate ion, Cr2O72-?
questions.explanation: Let Cr = x: 2x + 7(-2) = -2, so 2x - 14 = -2, 2x = 12, x = +6 for each chromium atom.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In the reaction Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, which species is the oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: Cu2+ is reduced to Cu (gains electrons), which means it oxidises the zinc; the oxidising agent is always the species that itself gets reduced.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In the same reaction, Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, zinc metal acts as the
options: oxidising agent, since it is oxidised
reducing agent, since it is oxidised
reducing agent, since it is reduced
questions.explanation: Zinc loses electrons (Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-), being oxidised itself, which makes it the reducing agent, since it causes the reduction of copper ions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in sulphuric acid, H2SO4?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following changes represents a reduction?
questions.explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons; Fe3+ gains one electron to become Fe2+, so this is a reduction half-equation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A redox reaction always involves
options: no change in oxidation number of any species
both oxidation and reduction occurring simultaneously
questions.explanation: Redox reactions are so named because reduction and oxidation always occur together, since electrons lost by one species must be gained by another.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of these is typically a strong oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: KMnO4 is a powerful oxidising agent because the manganese in the +7 oxidation state is readily reduced, accepting electrons from other species.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Electrolysis is the process by which
options: an electric current decomposes an ionic compound in molten or dissolved state
a compound decomposes purely on heating
a gas diffuses through a porous membrane
two solutions are mixed to form a precipitate
questions.explanation: Electrolysis passes direct current through a molten or dissolved electrolyte, driving ions to the electrodes where they are discharged and decomposed chemically.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: During electrolysis, positive ions (cations) migrate to the
questions.explanation: Cations are attracted to the negatively charged cathode, where they gain electrons (are reduced) to form neutral atoms or molecules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis states that the mass of a substance liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to
options: the quantity of electricity (charge) passed through the electrolyte
questions.explanation: Faraday's First Law: mass deposited/liberated = (charge passed) x (chemical equivalent)/Faraday constant, so mass is directly proportional to the charge passed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: One Faraday of electricity is equal to the charge carried by
questions.explanation: A Faraday (approximately 96,500 coulombs) is defined as the charge on one mole of electrons (Avogadro's number of electrons).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What mass of copper is deposited when a current of 2 amperes flows for 965 seconds through copper(II) sulphate solution? (1 Faraday = 96500 C, Cu = 64, deposition requires 2 electrons per Cu2+)
questions.explanation: Charge = It = 2 x 965 = 1930 C. Moles of electrons = 1930/96500 = 0.02. Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, so moles Cu = 0.02/2 = 0.01. Mass = 0.01 x 64 = 0.64 g.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Electroplating is an industrial application of electrolysis used mainly to
options: coat a metal object with a thin protective or decorative layer of another metal
extract reactive metals from their molten ores
questions.explanation: In electroplating, the object to be plated is made the cathode in a solution containing ions of the plating metal, which is deposited onto its surface.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which metal is commercially extracted by electrolysis of its molten oxide (dissolved in molten cryolite)?
questions.explanation: Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by carbon reduction, so its ore (bauxite, as Al2O3) is dissolved in molten cryolite and electrolysed (the Hall-Heroult process).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In the electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid using inert (platinum) electrodes, the gas liberated at the cathode is
questions.explanation: H+ ions are attracted to the cathode and reduced to hydrogen gas: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2, while oxygen is liberated at the anode from discharge of hydroxide/water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings, causing a rise in temperature, is described as
questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions release energy (enthalpy change is negative), warming the surroundings, as seen in combustion and neutralization reactions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings, causing a fall in temperature, is described as
questions.explanation: Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings (enthalpy change is positive), cooling the surroundings, as in the decomposition of calcium carbonate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: According to Le Chatelier's Principle, if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in conditions, the system will
options: remain completely unaffected by the change
always shift towards the products regardless of the change
shift in the direction that tends to oppose (counteract) that change
always shift towards the reactants regardless of the change
questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's Principle predicts that equilibrium position adjusts to minimise the effect of an imposed change in concentration, pressure, or temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In the reversible reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) + heat, increasing pressure will shift the equilibrium
options: towards the reactants, since there are fewer gas moles on that side
towards the products, only if a catalyst is present
towards the products, since there are fewer gas moles on that side
in no particular direction, since pressure has no effect
questions.explanation: There are 4 moles of gas on the reactant side and 2 on the product side; increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, shifting equilibrium towards NH3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In the same exothermic reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) + heat, increasing temperature will shift the equilibrium
options: completely to the products, converting all reactants
towards the reactants, since the forward reaction is exothermic
towards the products, since heat favours forward reaction
questions.explanation: By Le Chatelier's Principle, adding heat favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, so increasing temperature shifts an exothermic equilibrium back towards the reactants.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction by
options: shifting the position of equilibrium towards the products
providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
increasing the temperature of the reaction mixture
questions.explanation: Catalysts speed up reactions by lowering activation energy without being consumed, and importantly, they do not alter the equilibrium position, only how fast it is reached.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following factors does NOT generally increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant
questions.explanation: Lowering temperature reduces the kinetic energy and collision frequency of particles, decreasing (not increasing) reaction rate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur is called the
questions.explanation: Activation energy is the energy barrier that reacting particles must overcome during effective collisions for a reaction to proceed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Alkanes are described as saturated hydrocarbons because they contain
options: only single (C-C) covalent bonds between carbon atoms
at least one carbon-carbon triple bond
at least one carbon-carbon double bond
questions.explanation: Saturation in organic chemistry means the carbon skeleton has only single bonds, as in the alkane homologous series (general formula CnH2n+2).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the general formula for the alkene homologous series?
questions.explanation: Alkenes contain one C=C double bond, giving the general formula CnH2n, two hydrogens fewer per carbon than the corresponding saturated alkane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which functional group characterises the alkanols (alcohols)?
questions.explanation: Alkanols are identified by the hydroxyl functional group (-OH) attached to a saturated carbon chain, e.g., ethanol, CH3CH2OH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Alkanoic acids (carboxylic acids) are characterised by which functional group?
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group, -COOH, defines the alkanoic acid series, giving these compounds their characteristic acidic properties, e.g., ethanoic acid, CH3COOH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An ester is formed by the reaction between
options: an alkanoic acid and an alkanol
an alkanoic acid and an alkane
questions.explanation: Esterification is the condensation reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, catalysed by a strong acid, producing an ester and water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the IUPAC name of the hydrocarbon with the structural formula CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3?
questions.explanation: This is a straight-chain alkane with 4 carbon atoms and only single bonds, named butane according to IUPAC nomenclature rules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The reaction of an alkene with bromine water, causing the orange-brown colour to decolourise, is used to test for
options: unsaturation (a carbon-carbon double or triple bond)
the presence of an alcohol group
the presence of a carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: Alkenes rapidly decolourise bromine water via addition across the C=C double bond, distinguishing them from saturated alkanes, which do not react.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Petroleum (crude oil) is separated into useful fractions such as petrol, kerosene, and diesel mainly by
options: fractional distillation, based on differing boiling points
questions.explanation: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different chain lengths and boiling points, separated in a fractionating column into fractions like petrol, kerosene, and diesel.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Polymers such as polythene are formed from small repeating units called
questions.explanation: Polymerisation joins many small monomer units (e.g., ethene monomers forming polythene) into a large, repeating-unit macromolecule called a polymer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which type of polymerisation occurs when ethene monomers join together without the loss of any small molecule?
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation, unsaturated monomers like ethene simply add together across their double bonds, with no by-product formed, unlike condensation polymerisation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Iron is commercially extracted from its ore, haematite, in the blast furnace using which reducing agent?
questions.explanation: In the blast furnace, coke burns to form carbon monoxide, which reduces iron(III) oxide to molten iron: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which property of metals allows them to be hammered into sheets without breaking?
questions.explanation: Malleability is the ability of a metal to be beaten or rolled into thin sheets, due to layers of metal ions being able to slide over one another.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Aluminium is often used for aircraft bodies and overhead cables mainly because of its
options: low density combined with good strength and corrosion resistance
high reactivity with oxygen forming a flaking oxide
questions.explanation: Aluminium's light weight, decent tensile strength, and a tough, adherent oxide layer that resists further corrosion make it ideal for aircraft and cables.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Copper is widely used in electrical wiring mainly because of its
questions.explanation: Copper conducts electricity very efficiently and can be drawn into thin wires (ductility), making it the standard choice for household and industrial wiring.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Nitrogen gas is manufactured industrially into ammonia by the Haber process, mainly for use in
questions.explanation: Ammonia produced from nitrogen and hydrogen (Haber process) is used mainly as a raw material for nitrogenous fertilisers like ammonium sulphate and urea.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Chlorine gas is widely used in water treatment plants mainly for its
options: ability to remove suspended solids by sedimentation
questions.explanation: Chlorine is added to drinking water in controlled amounts because it kills disease-causing bacteria and other pathogens, making the water safe to drink.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In terms of bond energies, a reaction is exothermic overall when
options: the energy released in forming new bonds in the products exceeds the energy absorbed in breaking bonds in the reactants
equal energy is always absorbed and released
no bonds are broken or formed during the reaction
the energy absorbed in breaking bonds exceeds the energy released in forming new bonds
questions.explanation: A reaction is exothermic when more energy is released forming the new bonds of the products than was needed to break the bonds of the reactants, giving a net release of energy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which technique separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using a porous barrier?
questions.explanation: Filtration uses a porous barrier (filter paper) to retain insoluble solid particles while allowing the liquid to pass through as filtrate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A pure liquid boils at a constant, sharp temperature. The presence of an impurity typically causes the boiling point to
options: rise, and boiling occurs over a range of temperature
questions.explanation: Dissolved impurities raise the boiling point of a liquid and cause it to boil over a range rather than at one sharp, fixed temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a physical change?
questions.explanation: Melting of ice is a physical change because only the state changes (solid to liquid); no new substance is formed, unlike the other examples, which are chemical changes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Decantation is most suitable for separating
options: dyes present in a mixture of inks
a dissolved salt from its solution
a liquid from a settled insoluble solid by carefully pouring off the liquid
questions.explanation: Decantation involves gently pouring off a liquid from a settled solid residue, leaving the denser solid behind at the bottom of the vessel.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The Law of Conservation of Mass states that
options: equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules
elements of a compound combine in a fixed mass ratio
gases combine in simple whole-number volume ratios
mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
questions.explanation: This law states that the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products in a chemical reaction, since atoms are only rearranged, not created or destroyed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Avogadro's number, representing the number of particles in one mole of a substance, is approximately
questions.explanation: Avogadro's number, 6.02 x 10^23 per mole, is the fixed number of atoms, molecules, or ions present in one mole of any substance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The relative atomic mass of an element is defined relative to
options: the mass of one hydrogen atom
1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom
the mass of one oxygen-16 atom
the mass of one mole of electrons
questions.explanation: By modern convention, relative atomic masses are measured on a scale where one atom of carbon-12 is assigned a mass of exactly 12 units.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the molar mass of ammonium sulphate, (NH4)2SO4? (N = 14, H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the approximate percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonia, NH3? (N = 14, H = 1)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of NH3 = 17. Percentage nitrogen = (14/17) x 100 = 82.4%.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A compound has empirical formula CH2 and a molar mass of 56 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.explanation: Empirical formula mass of CH2 = 14. Since 56/14 = 4, the molecular formula is 4 times the empirical formula: C4H8.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A gas has a volume of 300 cm3 at 27 degC and 1 atmosphere pressure. What volume will it occupy at 127 degC and 2 atmospheres pressure?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Gas A diffuses twice as fast as gas B. If the molar mass of gas B is 64, what is the molar mass of gas A?
questions.explanation: By Graham's Law, rate_A/rate_B = sqrt(M_B/M_A). Since rate_A/rate_B = 2, M_B/M_A = 4, so M_A = 64/4 = 16.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An atom has a mass number of 39 and an atomic number of 19. How many neutrons does it contain?
questions.explanation: Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 39 - 19 = 20.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the electronic configuration of the Cl- ion? (Chlorine has atomic number 17)
questions.explanation: A chlorine atom (2,8,7) gains one electron to form Cl-, giving the stable configuration 2,8,8, the same as argon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Ionisation energy generally behaves as follows in the periodic table:
options: it decreases down a group and decreases across a period
it decreases down a group and increases across a period from left to right
it increases down a group and decreases across a period
it increases down a group and increases across a period
questions.explanation: Down a group, increased shielding and atomic radius make electron removal easier (lower ionisation energy); across a period, increasing nuclear charge makes it harder (higher ionisation energy).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Group I elements of the periodic table are commonly known as
questions.explanation: Group I elements (lithium, sodium, potassium, etc.) are called alkali metals because they react with water to form strongly alkaline hydroxide solutions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The weak intermolecular forces of attraction present between all molecules, including non-polar ones, are called
questions.explanation: Van der Waals forces are weak, temporary attractions arising from fluctuating electron distributions, present even between non-polar molecules like noble gas atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A bond between two atoms is generally considered ionic rather than covalent when the difference in electronegativity between them is
questions.explanation: A large electronegativity difference favours complete electron transfer (ionic bonding), while a small or zero difference favours electron sharing (covalent bonding).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The random, erratic movement of smoke particles observed under a microscope, caused by collisions with fast-moving air molecules, is called
questions.explanation: Brownian motion is the visible, random jittering of larger suspended particles caused by continuous, unequal bombardment from surrounding fast-moving molecules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The direct change of a substance from gas to solid, without passing through the liquid state, is called
questions.explanation: Deposition is the reverse of sublimation, occurring when a gas changes directly into a solid, as seen when water vapour forms frost.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the molarity of a solution containing 4 g of NaOH dissolved in 500 cm3 of solution? (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of NaOH = 40. Moles = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Molarity = moles/volume(dm3) = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 mol/dm3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: 50 cm3 of 2.0 mol/dm3 HCl is diluted with water to a total volume of 200 cm3. What is the concentration of the diluted solution?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The solubility of a gas in a liquid generally increases with
questions.explanation: Gas solubility rises with higher pressure (more gas forced into solution) and lower temperature (less kinetic energy for gas molecules to escape).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: During a chemical reaction, breaking bonds in the reactants requires an input of energy, while forming new bonds in the products
questions.explanation: Bond breaking always absorbs energy and bond formation always releases energy; whether the overall reaction is exothermic or endothermic depends on which effect dominates.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Entropy is best described as a measure of
options: the degree of disorder or randomness of a system
the heat capacity of a substance
the total energy content of a system
the rate of a chemical reaction
questions.explanation: Entropy quantifies the disorder or randomness of a system's particles; processes tend to proceed towards states of greater overall entropy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a classic reversible reaction studied at equilibrium?
options: combustion of magnesium ribbon in oxygen
rusting of iron in moist air
questions.explanation: The oxidation of sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide (used in the Contact Process) is a reversible reaction that reaches a dynamic equilibrium, unlike the other examples, which go to completion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Increasing the concentration of reactants in a solution increases the rate of reaction mainly because
options: it lowers the activation energy of the reaction
it increases the frequency of collisions between reacting particles
it changes the reaction mechanism entirely
it increases the temperature of the reaction mixture
questions.explanation: A higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, leading to more frequent effective collisions and hence a faster reaction rate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A reaction should theoretically produce 20 g of product, but only 15 g is actually obtained. What is the percentage yield?
questions.explanation: Percentage yield = (actual yield/theoretical yield) x 100 = (15/20) x 100 = 75%.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What volume, in dm3, is occupied by 0.2 mole of a gas at s.t.p.? (Molar volume = 22.4 dm3/mol)
questions.explanation: Volume = number of moles x molar volume = 0.2 x 22.4 = 4.48 dm3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the approximate density of carbon dioxide gas at s.t.p., in g/dm3? (CO2 molar mass = 44, molar volume = 22.4 dm3/mol)
questions.explanation: Density = molar mass/molar volume = 44/22.4 = 1.96 g/dm3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Chlorine has two isotopes, Cl-35 (75% abundance) and Cl-37 (25% abundance). What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a chemical property, not a physical property, of a substance?
questions.explanation: Flammability describes how a substance reacts (burns) with oxygen, forming new substances, whereas density, melting point, and colour can be observed without any chemical change occurring.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The process by which molecules of a gas or liquid spontaneously spread out to fill the space available to them is called
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration due to their random motion, until evenly spread throughout the space.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Dilute acids react with reactive metals such as zinc or magnesium to produce
options: only a salt, with no gas evolved
questions.explanation: Reactive metals displace hydrogen from dilute acids, forming a salt and releasing hydrogen gas, e.g., Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A strong acid is one that
options: always has a pH of exactly 7
does not ionise at all in water
questions.explanation: Strong acids like HCl and H2SO4 dissociate almost completely into ions in water, unlike weak acids such as ethanoic acid, which only partially ionise.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The basicity of an acid refers to
options: the number of replaceable hydrogen atoms per molecule of the acid
its strength as measured on the pH scale
the number of oxygen atoms in its formula
the number of hydroxide ions it produces in solution
questions.explanation: Basicity describes how many acidic (replaceable) hydrogen atoms an acid molecule has; for example, H2SO4 is dibasic, having two replaceable hydrogens.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An amphoteric oxide is one that can react chemically with
questions.explanation: Amphoteric oxides, such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide, can act as either an acid or a base, reacting with both acids and alkalis to form salts.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: An aqueous solution of ammonium chloride is slightly acidic because
options: the ammonium ion hydrolyses in water to release H+ ions
it is a salt of a strong acid and a strong base
the chloride ion hydrolyses in water to release OH- ions
questions.explanation: Ammonium chloride is a salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a weak base (NH3); the ammonium ion hydrolyses slightly, releasing H+ and making the solution acidic.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate crystals, CuSO4.5H2O, are heated until all water of crystallisation is driven off. The resulting anhydrous salt is
questions.explanation: Removing the water of crystallisation turns blue hydrated copper(II) sulphate into white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate powder.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A 5.0 g sample of hydrated magnesium sulphate, MgSO4.xH2O, is heated to constant mass, losing 2.56 g of water and leaving 2.44 g of anhydrous MgSO4. (MgSO4 = 120, H2O = 18). What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Moles of MgSO4 = 2.44/120 = 0.0203; moles of H2O = 2.56/18 = 0.1422. Ratio of H2O to MgSO4 = 0.1422/0.0203 is approximately 7, so x = 7, matching Epsom salt, MgSO4.7H2O.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in the nitrate ion, NO3-?
questions.explanation: Let nitrogen = x: x + 3(-2) = -1, so x - 6 = -1, giving x = +5.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What quantity of electricity (in coulombs) is required to deposit 5.4 g of silver from silver nitrate solution during electrolysis? (Ag = 108, 1 Faraday = 96500 C, Ag+ + e- -> Ag)
questions.explanation: Moles of Ag = 5.4/108 = 0.05 mol. Since one electron deposits one Ag atom, charge = 0.05 x 96500 = 4825 C.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr2, using inert electrodes, the reaction occurring at the anode is
questions.explanation: At the anode (positive electrode), bromide ions are oxidised (lose electrons) to form bromine gas, since molten PbBr2 has no water present.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Sodium metal is extracted industrially by electrolysis of
options: molten sodium chloride, in the Downs process
questions.explanation: Sodium is too reactive to extract by chemical reduction, so it is obtained by electrolysing molten sodium chloride in the industrial Downs process.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which method is used to extract a moderately reactive metal such as zinc or iron from its oxide ore?
options: The metal is found native and needs no extraction
Thermal decomposition alone, with no reducing agent
Chemical reduction with carbon or carbon monoxide
questions.explanation: Metals of moderate reactivity, like zinc and iron, are extracted by reducing their oxide ores with carbon or carbon monoxide, which is cheaper than electrolysis.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a noble (inert) gas found in trace amounts in the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Argon makes up about 0.93% of the atmosphere and, as a noble gas, is chemically unreactive under ordinary conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate is commonly used to test for the presence of water because, on contact with water, it turns from
questions.explanation: White anhydrous copper(II) sulphate absorbs water to reform hydrated blue copper(II) sulphate crystals, providing a simple visual test for water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Hydrogen gas is commonly prepared in the laboratory by reacting
options: manganese(IV) oxide with concentrated hydrochloric acid
zinc granules with dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Zinc, a reactive metal, displaces hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2, a standard laboratory preparation of hydrogen.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The characteristic laboratory test for hydrogen gas is that it
options: turns damp litmus paper red then bleaches it
burns with a 'pop' sound when a lighted splint is introduced
questions.explanation: Hydrogen gas gives a characteristic squeaky 'pop' sound when ignited with a lighted splint, distinguishing it from oxygen and other common gases.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Reactivity of the halogens (Group VII elements) generally
questions.explanation: Down Group VII, atomic radius increases and the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder to attract an extra electron, so reactivity decreases.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Chlorine gas bubbled through potassium bromide solution displaces bromine because
options: chlorine is less electronegative than bromine
chlorine is more reactive (a stronger oxidising agent) than bromine
bromine is more reactive than chlorine
questions.explanation: Being higher in Group VII, chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine and so displaces bromide ions to form bromine: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Oxygen gas is confirmed present in a test tube by testing with a
options: lighted splint, which it extinguishes with a pop
sample of limewater, which it turns milky
piece of damp red litmus paper, which it turns blue
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion, so a glowing splint inserted into a test tube of the gas will burst back into flame (relight).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Nitrogen gas is relatively unreactive at room temperature mainly because of
options: the strong triple covalent bond between its two nitrogen atoms
questions.explanation: The N triple bond N in the N2 molecule has very high bond energy, requiring a lot of energy to break, which makes nitrogen gas chemically inert under normal conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Diamond and graphite are both allotropes of carbon, yet graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not, because
options: graphite contains more carbon atoms per gram than diamond
diamond contains metallic impurities that block conduction
graphite has delocalised electrons that can move freely within its layers, unlike diamond's fully bonded structure
questions.explanation: In graphite, each carbon is bonded to only three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move and conduct electricity, unlike diamond, where all four electrons are localised in covalent bonds.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Carbon dioxide gas is confirmed by bubbling it through limewater, which turns
options: milky (cloudy) due to the formation of insoluble calcium carbonate
brown due to an oxidation reaction
blue due to the formation of a complex ion
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide (limewater) to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which clouds the solution: CO2 + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCO3 + H2O.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Rhombic sulphur and monoclinic sulphur are examples of
questions.explanation: Rhombic and monoclinic sulphur are different crystalline structural forms (allotropes) of the same element, sulphur, stable at different temperatures.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Sulphur dioxide gas can be identified by its ability to
options: turn acidified potassium dichromate(VI) paper from orange to green
produce a 'pop' sound with a lighted splint
turn limewater milky instantly and permanently
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide is a reducing agent that reduces orange dichromate(VI) ions to green chromium(III) ions, providing a characteristic test.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: When a small piece of sodium metal is added to water, it
options: dissolves completely with no chemical reaction
reacts violently to produce oxygen gas
floats, moves rapidly across the surface, and reacts to liberate hydrogen gas
questions.explanation: Sodium is less dense than water and reacts vigorously with it, darting across the surface while releasing hydrogen gas and forming sodium hydroxide: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Calcium oxide (quicklime) reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) in a reaction that is
options: not a chemical reaction at all
reversible only at very high pressure
questions.explanation: The reaction CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 releases a large amount of heat, making it strongly exothermic, sometimes enough to make the water boil.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Aluminium oxide, Al2O3, is described as amphoteric because it reacts chemically with
options: both acids and alkalis to form salts
questions.explanation: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids to form aluminium salts and with alkalis to form aluminates, demonstrating its amphoteric nature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Rusting of iron is best prevented by
options: exposing the iron to more oxygen
storing the iron permanently in water
coating the iron surface with paint, oil, or zinc (galvanising) to exclude air and moisture
questions.explanation: Rusting requires both oxygen and water; coating iron with paint, oil, or a protective zinc layer (galvanising) excludes these and prevents corrosion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A characteristic property of transition metals, distinguishing them from Group I and Group II metals, is that they
options: exist only in the +1 oxidation state
are more reactive than sodium and potassium
commonly exhibit variable oxidation states and form coloured compounds
questions.explanation: Transition metals typically show several oxidation states and form coloured compounds and ions, due to their partially filled d-orbitals, unlike the s-block metals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Brass is an alloy composed mainly of
questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, valued for its improved strength, workability, and corrosion resistance compared to pure copper.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Steel is an alloy of iron with a small, controlled percentage of
questions.explanation: Steel is produced by adding a controlled small amount of carbon to iron, which greatly increases its hardness and strength compared to pure iron.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Ammonia gas can be identified by its characteristic pungent smell and its ability to
options: turn damp blue litmus paper red
produce a 'pop' sound with a lighted splint
turn damp red litmus paper blue
questions.explanation: Ammonia is an alkaline gas that dissolves in the moisture on damp red litmus paper, turning it blue, which is a standard test for ammonia.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A homologous series is a group of organic compounds that
options: all have exactly the same molecular formula
contain only carbon and hydrogen atoms
are all gases at room temperature
have the same general formula and similar chemical properties, differing by a CH2 unit between successive members
questions.explanation: Members of a homologous series share a common general formula and similar chemical behaviour, with each successive member differing by one CH2 unit in molecular formula and mass.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Structural isomers are compounds that have
options: the same physical properties but different molecular formulas
the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements of atoms
the same number of carbon atoms only, with no other similarity
different molecular formulas but the same structural arrangement
questions.explanation: Structural isomers share an identical molecular formula but differ in how their atoms are bonded and arranged, giving them different properties.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Alkanones (ketones) are characterised by which functional group?
options: A carbonyl group bonded to at least one hydrogen atom
A carbonyl group, C=O, bonded to two carbon atoms
questions.explanation: In ketones, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two other carbon atoms (as in propanone, CH3COCH3), distinguishing them from aldehydes, where it is bonded to at least one hydrogen.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Alkanals (aldehydes) contain the functional group
options: -CHO, a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one hydrogen atom
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are identified by the -CHO group, where the carbonyl carbon is always bonded to at least one hydrogen atom, usually at the end of the carbon chain.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which functional group characterises the amines?
questions.explanation: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia containing the amino group, -NH2, attached to a carbon chain, e.g., methylamine, CH3NH2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the IUPAC name of CH3-CH2-CH2-OH?
questions.explanation: This is a three-carbon alcohol with the -OH group on the terminal (first) carbon, so it is named propan-1-ol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the name of the ester formed from the reaction of ethanoic acid with methanol?
questions.explanation: The alcohol (methanol) provides the alkyl part of the name (methyl), and the acid (ethanoic acid) provides the '-oate' part, giving methyl ethanoate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the general formula of the alkyne homologous series?
questions.explanation: Alkynes contain one carbon-carbon triple bond, giving the general formula CnH2n-2, four hydrogens fewer per carbon than the corresponding alkane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Alkynes, like alkenes, decolourise bromine water because they contain
options: only single bonds throughout the molecule
at least one carbon-carbon triple bond, which undergoes addition reactions
questions.explanation: The carbon-carbon triple bond in alkynes is a site of unsaturation that readily undergoes addition reactions with bromine, decolourising bromine water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Benzene, C6H6, has a structure best described as
options: a fully saturated six-membered ring with only single bonds
three completely separate, isolated double bonds
a planar ring of six carbon atoms with delocalised pi electrons above and below the ring
a straight chain of six carbon atoms with alternating fixed double bonds
questions.explanation: Benzene's six carbon atoms form a planar hexagonal ring with delocalised pi electrons spread evenly above and below the ring, giving all C-C bonds equal length and extra stability.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Benzene is more resistant to addition reactions than a typical alkene mainly because of
options: the complete absence of pi electrons in its structure
the delocalisation of its pi electrons around the ring, giving it extra stability
questions.explanation: The delocalised electron system in benzene lowers its overall energy (delocalisation/resonance stabilisation), making it favour substitution reactions over addition, unlike alkenes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Alkanes react with chlorine gas in the presence of ultraviolet light via
options: a substitution reaction, replacing hydrogen atoms with chlorine atoms
an addition reaction across a carbon-carbon double bond
questions.explanation: Since alkanes are saturated (no double bonds), chlorine substitutes for hydrogen atoms one at a time under UV light, forming chloroalkanes and hydrogen chloride.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Ethene reacts with hydrogen gas in the presence of a nickel catalyst to form
questions.explanation: Hydrogenation adds hydrogen across the C=C double bond of ethene, using a nickel catalyst, to produce the saturated hydrocarbon ethane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Ethene can be converted industrially to ethanol by reacting it with steam in the presence of
options: an alkaline solution, via a hydrolysis reaction
concentrated sulphuric acid only, via a substitution reaction
a phosphoric acid catalyst, in an addition (hydration) reaction
a nickel catalyst, via an elimination reaction
questions.explanation: In the catalytic hydration process, ethene and steam react over a phosphoric acid catalyst under pressure, adding water across the double bond to form ethanol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Ethanol can be produced biologically from glucose by fermentation using
options: bacteria, in the presence of excess oxygen
a nickel catalyst under high pressure
yeast (containing the enzyme zymase), in the absence of air
questions.explanation: During anaerobic fermentation, the zymase enzyme in yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide: C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: When ethanol is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI), it forms first ethanal and then, on further oxidation,
questions.explanation: Ethanol is oxidised in stages: first to the aldehyde, ethanal, then further to the carboxylic acid, ethanoic acid, by the acidified dichromate(VI) oxidising agent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Ethanol undergoes dehydration when heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid or passed over hot aluminium oxide, forming
questions.explanation: Dehydration removes a molecule of water from ethanol, forming the unsaturated hydrocarbon ethene: C2H5OH -> C2H4 + H2O.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A simple test to distinguish an alkanol from an alkanoic acid is to add a small amount of
options: water, which dissolves both compounds equally well
sodium carbonate, which produces effervescence (carbon dioxide gas) only with the acid
bromine water, which decolourises with both compounds
universal indicator, which shows the same colour with both compounds
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide gas (effervescence), while neutral alkanols show no such reaction, providing a simple distinguishing test.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Catalytic cracking of long-chain hydrocarbons is the process of
options: joining small hydrocarbon molecules into larger polymer chains
distilling crude oil into separate fractions
breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones, including alkenes
removing sulphur impurities from crude oil
questions.explanation: Cracking breaks large, less useful hydrocarbon molecules from heavier fractions into smaller alkanes and alkenes, which are in greater industrial demand.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Cracking of hydrocarbon fractions from crude oil is carried out mainly because
options: cracking increases the boiling point of the fractions produced
smaller hydrocarbons cannot be used as fuels at all
larger hydrocarbons burn more efficiently as fuel without modification
there is greater industrial demand for smaller, more volatile hydrocarbons like petrol than for larger ones
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation of crude oil yields more heavy fractions than the market demands, so cracking converts the excess into smaller, more commercially valuable hydrocarbons such as petrol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Soap is manufactured by heating animal or vegetable fat with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution in a process called
options: cracking, which breaks the fat into smaller molecules
esterification, which forms an ester and water
saponification, which hydrolyses the fat into soap and glycerol
questions.explanation: Saponification is the alkaline hydrolysis of a fat (triglyceride) by sodium hydroxide, producing soap (sodium salts of fatty acids) and glycerol as a by-product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Carbohydrates are organic compounds composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, typically with hydrogen and oxygen present in the same ratio as in
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates such as glucose, C6H12O6, have hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 ratio, the same ratio found in water, which is the basis of the name 'hydrate of carbon'.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Glucose can be identified as a reducing sugar by warming it with Fehling's solution, which changes colour from
questions.explanation: Reducing sugars like glucose reduce the blue copper(II) ions in Fehling's solution to a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide on warming.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Proteins are natural polymers made up of monomer units called
questions.explanation: Proteins are condensation polymers formed by linking many amino acid monomers together in long chains.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The bond linking amino acids together in a protein chain is called a
questions.explanation: A peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, releasing water in a condensation reaction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Complete hydrolysis of a fat (triglyceride) yields
options: glycerol and three fatty acid molecules
questions.explanation: A triglyceride (fat) is an ester of glycerol and three fatty acids; hydrolysis breaks the ester bonds, releasing free glycerol and three fatty acid molecules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The presence of starch in a food sample is confirmed by adding a few drops of
questions.explanation: Iodine solution forms a characteristic blue-black complex with starch molecules, providing a simple and specific test for starch.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a naturally occurring polymer, unlike synthetic polymers such as polythene?
questions.explanation: Starch is a natural polymer made of many glucose units joined together, whereas PVC, polystyrene, and nylon are all synthetic, man-made polymers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Butane, C4H10, has how many structural isomers?
questions.explanation: Butane exists as two structural isomers with the molecular formula C4H10: the straight-chain n-butane and the branched 2-methylpropane (isobutane).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Complete combustion of an alkane in excess oxygen produces
options: carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas only
questions.explanation: With sufficient oxygen, alkanes burn completely to give carbon dioxide and water as the only products, e.g., CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The main component of natural gas is
questions.explanation: Natural gas is predominantly methane (typically over 90%), with smaller amounts of ethane, propane, and other hydrocarbons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the IUPAC name of the branched alkane (CH3)2CH-CH2-CH3?
questions.explanation: This C5H12 isomer has a methyl branch on the second carbon of a four-carbon (butane) chain, so it is named 2-methylbutane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Methanol is added to ethanol to produce methylated spirit mainly in order to
options: increase the boiling point of the ethanol
make the ethanol unfit for drinking (denature it), for industrial and tax purposes
make the ethanol react faster with acids
make the ethanol burn with a coloured flame
questions.explanation: Methanol and other additives are mixed with ethanol intended for industrial use to make it toxic and unpalatable (denatured), preventing its consumption as a beverage and avoiding alcohol duties.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Amines behave as weak bases in aqueous solution because the nitrogen atom's lone pair of electrons can
options: form a coordinate bond with oxygen atoms only
accept a proton (H+) from water, forming an ammonium-type ion
donate an electron to form a covalent bond with another amine
questions.explanation: The lone pair on the nitrogen atom of an amine can accept a proton from water, generating an alkylammonium ion and hydroxide ions, giving amines their weakly basic character.
